name: D1.0 The basic words of cybersecurity

paragraphes: Your phone holds your photos, your messages and your secrets. You lock it with a code.
Without knowing it, you already do security: you protect what matters to you.
A company does the same thing, but with thousands of devices and files. Protecting all of that is called cybersecurity.

decouverte.comme: A house is not protected by just one thing. There is the door, the lock, the alarm and watchful neighbors.
decouverte.enVrai: In cybersecurity, you also combine three things: people, work rules and tools. None of them is enough alone. A house has a door you can see, but the doors of a computer system are sometimes invisible.

decouverte.question: In a company, who is responsible for security?
options: Everyone, from the director to the intern
decouverte.answer: Everyone, from the director to the intern
decouverte.explanation: The official manual says security is everyone's job, from the director to the newest employee. The other two answers are tempting: people think it is a job for specialists. One mistake by one employee can be enough to cause a problem.

decouverte.titre: The CISSP, a diploma for security
decouverte.texte: The CISSP is a certification: a respected diploma that proves you know information security well. An organization called (ISC)2 awards it. To keep it, you must follow rules of good conduct.

decouverte.comme: To visit a big country, you split it into regions. You explore them one by one.
decouverte.enVrai: The CISSP program is split into eight domains. This course starts with domain 1: security and risk management. Before that, you learn the basic words.

cards.question: What is cybersecurity?
cards.answer: It means protecting information and computers. You protect them from unwanted access, changes and breakdowns. Example: the code that locks your phone.
cards.explanation: Think of your phone code: it stops other people from seeing and changing your things.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual (domain 1) talks about protecting information and systems. It mentions inappropriate access, use, modification and disruption.

cards.question: What is information security?
cards.answer: It has the same goal as cybersecurity: protecting information and the machines that hold it. The CISSP manual mostly uses this name.
cards.explanation: Two names for the same idea. In this course, you can treat them as synonyms.

cards.question: To protect a company well, what matters most?
cards.answer: Combining people, rules and tools
cards.explanation: A tool alone can be bypassed or used badly. People and rules close the other doors.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual insists: a strong security program is more than a collection of tools. It needs processes and oversight.

cards.question: What is the CISSP?
cards.answer: It is a respected certification in information security. It proves you know this job well. You follow its program in this course.
cards.explanation: A certification is a diploma you take to prove your skills.
cards.explanation_more: CISSP stands for Certified Information Systems Security Professional (outside the manual: full name of the certification).

cards.question: What is (ISC)2?
cards.answer: It is the organization that awards the CISSP certification. It also publishes the manual this course follows.
cards.explanation: A member who does not follow the code of ethics can lose the certification.
cards.explanation_more: Source: domain 1 of the manual, start of the chapter on ethics.

cards.question: In a company, which sentence describes security best?
options: It concerns only the IT team
options_why: Specialists lead it, but every employee can cause a problem or prevent one.
Managers set the direction, but everyone follows the rules.
cards.answer: It concerns all employees
cards.explanation: From the director to the newest employee: everyone has a role to play.

cards.question: Cybersecurity relies on three things: [[people]], [[rules|processes]] and tools.
cards.answer: Cybersecurity relies on three things: people, rules and tools.
cards.explanation: The three work together: each one makes up for the weak points of the others.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual says “people, processes, and technologies”.

cards.question: Why is one protection not enough?
cards.answer: Because one protection can break down or be bypassed. With several layers, other barriers remain when one gives way.
cards.explanation: Like in a house: the door, the lock and the alarm take turns.

cards.question: How many domains does the CISSP program have?
cards.answer: Eight. This course starts with domain 1: Security and Risk Management.
cards.explanation: Each domain is a big region of the program.
cards.explanation_more: Source: outline of the (ISC)2 manual that this course follows, eight domains.

cards.question: Which box does each example go in?
cards.answer: People: training and reporting. Rules: the document and the procedure. Tools: the lock and the alarm.
cards.explanation: Ask yourself: is it someone, an instruction, or an object?

items.text: Training employees to spot traps
An employee who reports a suspicious message
A document that says who can enter the office
A procedure for welcoming a new employee
An electronic lock on the office door
An alarm that rings when someone forces the entrance

cards.question: Lea gets a strange message from a coworker. Instead of ignoring it, she warns the security team. What does her action show?
options: Every employee plays a role in security
Only experts should report a problem
A strange message only concerns IT
options_why: Anyone can spot a problem, not just experts.
A strange message can affect the whole company, not just the machines.
cards.answer: Every employee plays a role in security
cards.explanation: Warning quickly helps limit the damage before it spreads.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual asks users to report any actual or suspected security breach.

cards.question: Can a simple employee mistake be enough to create a security problem?
options: Yes, even with no bad person involved
No, there must always be a bad person
cards.answer: Yes, even with no bad person involved
cards.explanation: An email sent to the wrong person is enough: no intention to harm is needed.

cards.question: Why do people say that people are the weakest link in security?
cards.answer: Because one human mistake is enough: clicking a trap link or sending a file to the wrong person. Well trained, they become the best protection.
cards.explanation: The weakest link is also the one you can strengthen by training people.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual says a company's security is only as strong as its weakest link, often its staff.

cards.question: What if a company only bought tools, without training its employees?
cards.answer: The tools would still be useful, but a human mistake could bypass them. Two pillars would be missing: people and rules.
cards.explanation: A tool does not replace an employee who knows what to do.

decouverte.titre: The phone that will not turn on
paragraphes: Your phone will not turn on. Maybe the screen is broken. Or maybe a program is stuck.
In the first case, the problem is the part you can touch. In the second, it is the part you cannot touch.
The first is called hardware. The second is called software.

decouverte.titre: A piano and its sheet music
decouverte.comme: The piano is the object you touch. The sheet music says which notes to play. Without sheet music, the piano stays silent.
decouverte.enVrai: Hardware is the computer itself: screen, keyboard, electronic parts. Software is the instructions that tell it what to do. The image stops here: you can copy software with one click, but not a piano.

decouverte.question: Is a video game hardware or software?
decouverte.explanation: The game is a set of instructions, so it is software. The console that runs it is the hardware. People often think the game is an object inside the console, but it is instructions.

decouverte.comme: In a restaurant kitchen, the head chef shares out the work and checks that everything goes well.
decouverte.enVrai: The operating system (OS) does this job inside a computer. Windows, macOS and Linux are examples. It links the hardware and the applications.

decouverte.titre: The customers of an online shop
decouverte.texte: An online shop records the name, address and orders of each customer. Each piece of saved information is data. Stored in an organized way, data forms a database. If someone changes it by mistake, the shop sends the wrong package.

cards.question: What is data?
cards.answer: Data is information stored in a computer: a name, a photo, a number. Example: your birth date in a form.
cards.explanation: For security, data is often the thing with the most value.

cards.question: What is a file?
cards.answer: A file is a set of data stored under one name. Example: a photo, a document or a spreadsheet.
cards.explanation: A folder is a place where you keep several files.

cards.question: The touch screen of your phone: hardware or software?
cards.answer: Hardware
cards.explanation: You can touch it: it is hardware. The software is what appears on it.

cards.question: What is hardware?
cards.answer: Hardware is the part of a computer that you can touch. Example: the screen, the keyboard, the disk that stores the files.
cards.explanation: It can break down, be stolen or be damaged.

cards.question: What is software?
cards.answer: Software is a set of instructions that tells the computer what to do. It is also called a program. Example: a word processor.
cards.explanation: It has no physical shape: you can only copy it or delete it.

cards.question: [[Hardware]] is the part you can touch; [[software]] is a set of instructions.
cards.answer: Hardware is the part you can touch; software is a set of instructions.
cards.explanation: Think of the piano and its sheet music.

cards.question: What is an application?
cards.answer: An application is software made for one specific task. Example: a messaging tool, a game or a calculator.
cards.explanation: On a phone, people often say an app.

cards.question: What is an operating system (OS)?
cards.answer: It is the main software of a computer. It links the hardware and the applications. Examples: Windows, macOS, Linux.
cards.explanation: Without it, applications would not know how to talk to the hardware.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions Windows, macOS and Linux: a company that uses several of them must protect them all.

cards.question: Which of these is an operating system?
options_why: A USB stick is an object you can touch: it is hardware.
A spreadsheet program is used to do calculations: it is an application.
cards.answer: Linux
cards.explanation: Linux links the hardware and the applications.

cards.question: What is a database?
cards.answer: A database is a large set of data stored in an organized way. Example: the customers of an online shop.
cards.explanation: You can search, add or change a piece of information very fast.

cards.question: What is a system?
cards.answer: It is a set of hardware and software that work together. Example: a store checkout, with its screen, its scanner and its program.
cards.explanation: When you protect a system, you protect all its parts at once.

cards.question: Hardware, software or data?
cards.answer: Hardware: the keyboard and the screen. Software: Windows and the game. Data: the name and the photo.
cards.explanation: If you can touch it, it is hardware. If it gives orders, it is software. If it describes something, it is data.

items.text: The keyboard
The screen of a computer
Windows
A game installed on your phone
Your name in a form
A vacation photo

cards.question: Why is it serious if a database is changed by mistake?
cards.answer: Because the company relies on this data to act. If it is incorrect, the company sends the wrong package or bills the wrong amount.
cards.explanation: Incorrect data leads to bad decisions.

cards.question: An online shop keeps the names, addresses and orders of its customers, stored in rows. What is this set called?
options_why: The operating system is the main software of the computer, not a set of customers.
An application is used to do a task. Here, we are talking about the data itself, neatly stored.
cards.answer: A database
cards.explanation: Neatly stored data that you can search quickly: that is a database.

cards.question: What if a computer had no operating system?
cards.answer: The hardware would be there, but no application could use it. The operating system links the two.
cards.explanation: It translates the requests of the applications for the hardware.

concepts.name: Networks, the internet and the cloud

paragraphes: You send a message to a friend on the other side of the world. It arrives in a few seconds. Yet your phones are not joined by a direct wire.
Between you, there is a huge web of cables, machines and relays. Your message passes from one to the next until it reaches its goal.
Devices linked together to exchange data form a network.

decouverte.comme: Roads link cities. Cars carry people or packages from one place to another.
decouverte.enVrai: A network links computers. Data travels like the cars. The internet is the worldwide network: millions of networks linked together.

decouverte.question: When you open a website, where are its pages stored?
options: On a powerful computer, somewhere in the world
decouverte.answer: On a powerful computer, somewhere in the world
decouverte.explanation: The pages are stored on a computer that stays on and answers all requests. It is called a server. Your phone only shows them, and your box connects you without keeping the pages.

decouverte.comme: In a restaurant, the cooks prepare the dishes that customers order. The kitchen stays open and serves many people.
decouverte.enVrai: A server is a computer that answers the requests of other devices. You ask for a page, and it sends it. It stays on day and night.

decouverte.comme: You do not keep everything at home. You rent space in a storage unit, and you pay for what you use.
decouverte.enVrai: Cloud computing rents out servers from companies. These servers are kept in big buildings called datacenters. The cloud is not a cloud in the sky: it is real machines.

decouverte.texte: In an office, employees share their files on a server. Some of their tools run in the cloud. When the internet connection goes down, they can no longer work with those tools.

cards.question: What is a network?
cards.answer: A network is a set of devices linked to exchange data. Example: the computers of a school, linked together.
cards.explanation: If one device on the network is attacked, the others can be hit too.

cards.question: What is the internet?
cards.answer: The internet is the worldwide network that links millions of networks. Example: the place where websites are found.
cards.explanation: A device connected to the internet can be reached from all over the world.

cards.question: Is the internal network of a school “the internet”?
options: No, it is one network among many
Yes, every network is the internet
cards.answer: No, it is one network among many
cards.explanation: The internet links millions of networks. A small network may not even be linked to the internet.

cards.question: What is a server?
cards.answer: A server is a computer that answers the requests of other devices. Example: the one that sends the pages of a website.
cards.explanation: It stays on all the time: it is an interesting target for attackers.

cards.question: What is an Internet service provider (ISP)?
cards.answer: It is the company that connects you to the internet. Example: the company behind the internet box in your home.
cards.explanation: If your provider goes down, you lose the internet.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions ISPs when it talks about redundancy: some companies rent several of them.

cards.question: In a company, employees share files on a computer that is always on. What is it called?
options_why: The internet service provider is the company that connects you to the internet, not the machine that keeps the files.
The operating system is the main software of a computer. Here, we are talking about the machine.
cards.answer: A server
cards.explanation: A machine that answers the requests of other devices is a server.

cards.question: What is the cloud (cloud computing)?
cards.answer: The cloud means using rented servers, located elsewhere, through the internet. Example: keeping your photos online.
cards.explanation: It is not a cloud in the sky: it is real machines in real buildings.

cards.question: What is a datacenter?
cards.answer: It is a big building full of servers. It needs electricity, cooling and a good connection.
cards.explanation: It holds a lot of data: it must be protected from breakdowns, fire and intruders.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions power failures, floods and excessive heat as threats to datacenters.

cards.question: The cloud means rented [[servers]], kept in [[datacenters]] and used through the internet.
cards.answer: The cloud means rented servers, kept in datacenters and used through the internet.
cards.explanation: Rented, far away, through the internet: three words to remember it.

cards.question: What is a cloud service provider (CSP)?
cards.answer: It is the company that rents out its servers to other companies. Example: a big company that hosts thousands of websites.
cards.explanation: When you use the cloud, part of the security depends on this provider.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual says that, in the cloud, the risk is shared between the customer and the provider.

cards.question: What is a virtual private network (VPN)?
cards.answer: It is a protected tunnel that links your device to a remote network, through the internet. Example: working from home on your company's network.
cards.explanation: The data inside this tunnel is hidden from snoopers.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions the VPN among the systems shared across a whole company.

cards.question: Put the journey of a web page in order.
cards.answer: You type the address. Your request goes to your internet provider. It crosses the internet. A server receives it. It sends back the page. It appears on your screen.
cards.explanation: Each step is a place where data can be read, changed or blocked.

items: You type the address of a website
Your request goes to your internet provider
The server sends back the page
The page appears on your screen

cards.question: An employee works from a cafe. What can they use to reach their company's files safely?
options: The cafe Wi-Fi, with nothing else
Sending the files to their phone in a message
options_why: A public Wi-Fi can be listened to by other people. It needs extra protection.
A message does not protect the files, and they leave the company's control.
cards.answer: A VPN
cards.explanation: The VPN creates a protected tunnel between the employee and the company network.

cards.question: Why does the breakdown of a datacenter affect many companies at once?
cards.answer: Because many companies rent the same servers. If those machines stop, all their customers lose their services at the same time.
cards.explanation: Putting all your eggs in one basket makes a breakdown hit harder.

cards.question: What if your internet provider went down?
cards.answer: Your devices would stay on, but they could no longer reach the internet. You could not open websites or use the cloud.
cards.explanation: Your connection depends on it: that is why some companies rent two.

concepts.name: Identity: account, password and rights (account, password, access)

paragraphes: At the school entrance, the supervisor looks at your card and lets you in. Yet he does not let you into the teachers' room.
He did two things. First, he checked that you are really you. Then, he decided where you are allowed to go.
A computer does the same: you prove who you are, then the system decides what you can do.

decouverte.comme: At school, everyone has a locker with their name on it. The padlock only opens with your code.
decouverte.enVrai: An account is your personal place in a system. The username says who it belongs to. The password is the secret code that proves it is you.

decouverte.question: Someone uses your password. What does the system believe?
options: That a stranger is trying to get in
That it must ask for a photo
decouverte.explanation: The system cannot see your face: it only sees the password. That is why a stolen password is so dangerous. The other answers are tempting, but the system has no way to guess.

decouverte.titre: Two proofs are better than one
decouverte.comme: To open a safe, you sometimes need a key and a code. If a thief only has the key, the safe stays closed.
decouverte.enVrai: Multifactor authentication (MFA) asks for several proofs. For example, a password and a code sent to your phone. Stealing the password is no longer enough.

decouverte.texte: In a company, an accountant can see the invoices. A technician can install programs. Access rights, also called permissions, say what each person can see or do. The administrator is the person with the widest rights on a system.

cards.question: What is an account?
cards.answer: An account is your personal place in a system. It lets you be recognized and use a service. Example: your email account.
cards.explanation: Each account belongs to one person or one service.

cards.question: What is a password?
cards.answer: A password is a secret that proves you are the real owner of the account. The longer and more unique it is, the better it protects.
cards.explanation: It must never be shared, or reused on several accounts.

cards.question: Which one must stay secret: the username or the password?
cards.answer: The password
cards.explanation: The username says who you are, and it is often known. The password is the proof: it must stay secret.

cards.question: What is a username (user ID)?
cards.answer: A username is the name that shows who an account belongs to. Example: your email address. It is usually not secret.
cards.explanation: Each person should have their own username, so you know who did what.
cards.explanation_more: Source: requirement 8 of PCI DSS, quoted in the manual (domain 1), asks for a unique ID for each person who uses a computer.

cards.question: What is authentication?
cards.answer: Authentication is the act of proving that you are who you say you are. Example: typing your password.
cards.explanation: Saying who you are is not enough: you must prove it.

cards.question: Proving who you are is called [[authentication]]. Deciding what you can do is called [[authorization]].
cards.answer: Proving who you are is called authentication. Deciding what you can do is called authorization.
cards.explanation: You prove first, you decide after: always in this order.

cards.question: What is multifactor authentication (MFA)?
cards.answer: It is authentication with at least two different proofs. Example: a password and a code sent to your phone.
cards.explanation: A thief who knows your password does not have your phone.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions it among the measures that protect access to sensitive data.

cards.question: What is single sign-on (SSO)?
cards.answer: It lets you identify yourself once to reach several services. Example: one account for the email and the documents.
cards.explanation: It is handy, but that account becomes very valuable: if it is stolen, everything opens.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual (domain 1): a useful idea for the rest of the course.

cards.question: An account asks for your password, then a code sent to your phone. What is this method called?
options_why: Authorization decides what you can do, not who you are.
Single sign-on lets you identify yourself once for several services: it is not the same idea.
cards.answer: Multifactor authentication
cards.explanation: Two different proofs: a secret you know and an object you have.

cards.question: What is authorization?
cards.answer: Authorization decides what you are allowed to do once you are identified. Example: reading a folder without being able to change it.
cards.explanation: Being recognized does not give you every right.

cards.question: A student shows a card at the entrance, then the supervisor tells them where they can go. Which step is authorization?
cards.answer: Saying where they can go
cards.explanation: Showing the card proves who they are: that is authentication. Deciding where they can go is authorization.

cards.question: What are access rights (permissions)?
cards.answer: Access rights are the list of what an account can see or do. They are also called privileges.
cards.explanation: The more rights an account has, the more dangerous it is if it is stolen.

cards.question: What is an administrator?
cards.answer: An administrator is the person who manages a system and has the widest rights. Example: the technician who installs the programs.
cards.explanation: Their account is very valuable: it must be protected first.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual also writes sysadmin, short for system administrator.

cards.question: Authentication or authorization?
cards.answer: Authentication: the password, the code and the fingerprint. Authorization: reading without changing, reaching the salaries, not installing.
cards.explanation: Authentication: who are you? Authorization: what are you allowed to do?

items.text: Typing your password
Entering a code sent to your phone
Placing your finger on a fingerprint reader
Being able to read a folder without changing it
Having access to the salaries folder
Not being allowed to install a program

cards.question: What is access control?
cards.answer: Access control is all the means that decide who can go where. Examples: badge, password, access rights.
cards.explanation: It can protect a room, a file or a program.

cards.question: Why is a password alone risky?
cards.answer: Because it can be guessed, stolen or reused. Whoever has it pretends to be you, and the system does not notice.
cards.explanation: Adding a second proof makes a stolen password almost useless.

cards.question: Tom moved from accounting to marketing, but he still has access to the invoices. What is the problem?
options: He has more rights than he needs
He does not have enough rights
options_why: On the contrary: he keeps rights he no longer needs.
Nothing in the situation talks about his password.
cards.answer: He has more rights than he needs
cards.explanation: When someone changes jobs, you remove the rights they no longer need.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual recommends removing access that is no longer needed when an employee transfers.

cards.question: What if everyone in the company had an administrator account?
cards.answer: Anyone could see or change everything. A mistake, or a stolen account, would do much more damage.
cards.explanation: Every extra right is an open door for no reason.

paragraphes: You pass a secret note to your friend during class. If the teacher catches it, they read it. So you invent a code: each letter is replaced by the next one.
The teacher reads “Cpokpvs” and understands nothing. Your friend steps back one letter and finds “Bonjour”.
Making a message unreadable is called encrypting. Turning it back into plain text is called decrypting.

decouverte.titre: The key is the secret of the code
decouverte.comme: Your “move one letter forward” code only works if the other person knows the rule. Without the rule, the message makes no sense.
decouverte.enVrai: In real encryption, the method is known to everyone. The secret is the key: a very long string of numbers. Without the right key, the message stays unreadable.

decouverte.question: A thief catches an encrypted message. Without the key, can they read it?
options: No, it stays unreadable without the key
decouverte.answer: No, it stays unreadable without the key
decouverte.explanation: Good encryption makes the text impossible to understand. The thief has the message, but nothing to read it with. Staring at it for a long time changes nothing.

decouverte.texte: When you pay online, your card data travels encrypted. A thief who catches it on the way only sees text that makes no sense. Only the shop's website has the key to decrypt it.

decouverte.comme: A fingerprint identifies a person. If the person changes, the fingerprint changes.
decouverte.enVrai: A hash is a short code calculated from a file. If you change a single letter of the file, the code changes completely. This way, you can tell that a file was modified. Warning: you cannot get the file back from its hash.

cards.question: What does it mean to encrypt?
cards.answer: To encrypt means to change a message so that it becomes unreadable without the key. Example: your card data during an online payment.
cards.explanation: The message still exists, but nobody can understand it without the key.

cards.question: What does it mean to decrypt?
cards.answer: To decrypt means to turn an encrypted message back into plain text, using the right key. It is the opposite of encrypting.
cards.explanation: Only the intended receivers have the key to do it.

cards.question: Making a message readable again with the key: encrypt or decrypt?
cards.answer: Decrypt
cards.explanation: Encrypting makes the message unreadable. Decrypting gives it back as readable text.

cards.question: What is an encryption key?
cards.answer: A key is a long string of numbers and letters used to encrypt or decrypt. It must stay secret.
cards.explanation: The method is known to everyone: all the secret is in the key.

cards.question: What are plaintext and ciphertext?
cards.answer: Plaintext can be read by anyone. Ciphertext is the result of encryption: it is unreadable without the key.
cards.explanation: Sending in plain text means sending with no protection at all.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual talks about sending sensitive emails “in the clear”: without encryption.

cards.question: An employee sends the salary list in a message, without encrypting it. How does the message travel?
options_why: Encrypted would mean a key made the message unreadable, which is not the case here.
Decrypted describes the act of turning a message back into plain text, not the way it travels.
cards.answer: In the clear
cards.explanation: Without encryption, anyone can read the message on the way.

cards.question: What is encryption?
cards.answer: Encryption is the technique of encrypting data. It stops a thief from reading what they copied.
cards.explanation: It is one of the most important protection measures.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions encryption among the measures that protect data.

cards.question: What is cryptography?
cards.answer: Cryptography is the science of secret codes. It creates encryption methods and studies how strong they are.
cards.explanation: Encryption is the tool, cryptography is the science behind it.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual (domain 1): a simple definition for the rest of the course.

cards.question: To read an [[encrypted]] message, you need the right [[key]].
cards.answer: To read an encrypted message, you need the right key.
cards.explanation: Without the key, even a stolen message stays unreadable.

cards.question: What is a hash?
cards.answer: It is a short code calculated from a file. If the file changes by a single character, the code changes too.
cards.explanation: You compare the codes to find out if a file was modified.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions cryptographic hashes among the measures that protect the accuracy of data.

cards.question: Encryption or hash: which one lets you get the original text back?
cards.answer: Encryption
cards.explanation: With the key, you decrypt. A hash cannot be turned back into a file: it is only used to compare.

cards.question: Encryption or hash?
cards.answer: Encryption: making unreadable, protecting a payment, reading with a key. Hash: comparing codes, spotting a change, getting the same code.
cards.explanation: Encryption hides the content. A hash spots a change.

items.text: Making an attachment unreadable for a thief
Protecting card data during a payment
Using a secret key to read a message
Comparing two codes to know if a file changed
Spotting that a document was secretly modified
Always getting the same short code for the same file

cards.question: Why encrypt data when a password already protects it?
cards.answer: Because a thief can copy the data without going through the password. Once encrypted, it stays unreadable for them.
cards.explanation: The password guards the door. Encryption protects the content, even if the door is bypassed.

cards.question: A laptop full of customer files is stolen on a train. What makes the data useless to the thief?
options_why: A complicated name does not stop anyone from opening the folder.
A wallpaper does not protect any data.
cards.answer: Encrypting the data
cards.explanation: Without the key, the content stays unreadable, even if the thief copies everything.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual lists forgetting to encrypt sensitive data as a human mistake that threatens its secrecy.

cards.question: What if the encryption key fell into the hands of a thief?
cards.answer: They could decrypt all the data. A key must therefore stay secret and well guarded.
cards.explanation: It is like a house key: if it is copied, the lock is no use anymore.

concepts.name: Attackers and their weapons (hackers, malware, phishing)

paragraphes: You get a message: “Your account is blocked. Click here to unblock it.” It has the logo of your bank. You panic a little.
But this message does not come from your bank. Someone wrote it to make you type your password on a fake website.
This trap is called phishing. Hackers, people who get into systems without permission, use it a lot.

decouverte.titre: The angler with a fishing rod
decouverte.comme: An angler throws out some bait. They do not force the fish: the fish chooses to bite.
decouverte.enVrai: The attacker is the one who carries out the attack. In phishing, the message is the bait: you open the door yourself by clicking. This is social engineering: tricking a person to get information.

decouverte.question: A stranger calls an employee and says they are from the IT team. They ask for the employee's password for a check. What does a good employee do?
options: They give it: it is the IT team
They give only half of the password
decouverte.explanation: A real IT team never asks for your password. Giving half is tempting, but it already gives the attacker a clue.

decouverte.comme: A flu virus sticks to one person and passes to the next. It needs a host to live.
decouverte.enVrai: A computer virus attaches itself to a file. When you open that file, it copies itself elsewhere. Malware (malicious software) is the general word for all programs made to cause harm. A virus is only one type.

decouverte.titre: Ransomware, a locked chest with no key
decouverte.comme: A thief locks your things in a chest. They only give you the key if you pay.
decouverte.enVrai: Ransomware encrypts your files to lock them. The attacker asks for money in return for the key. You get your files back if you pay, or if you kept a copy elsewhere.

decouverte.texte: A concert ticket website receives millions of requests in the same second. It can no longer answer the real customers. This attack is called a denial of service (DoS).

cards.question: What is a hacker?
cards.answer: A hacker is a person who tries to get into a system without having the right to. This is the meaning the word has in this course.
cards.explanation: The word sometimes also means a computer expert, but here it means the intruder.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual uses “hacker” for a person who attacks a system, for example to encrypt data and ask for a ransom.

cards.question: What is an attack?
cards.answer: An attack is a deliberate action to steal, change or block data or a system. The person who carries it out is the attacker.
cards.explanation: The common point: someone acts on purpose to cause harm.

cards.question: A hacker tries passwords on an account that is not theirs. Is this already an attack?
options: Yes, even if they broke nothing
No, they have not broken anything yet
cards.answer: Yes, even if they broke nothing
cards.explanation: An attack is a deliberate action to cause harm. Trying to get in without the right is already one.

cards.question: What is malware (malicious software)?
cards.answer: Malware is a program made to cause harm: stealing, damaging or blocking data. Examples: virus, ransomware, Trojan horse.
cards.explanation: Malware comes from the words malicious software.

cards.question: What is a computer virus?
cards.answer: A virus is malware that attaches itself to a file and copies itself when you open that file. This way, it passes from file to file.
cards.explanation: Like a flu virus, it needs a host to spread.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions viruses among the threats that can change or damage data.

cards.question: Is a virus a kind of malware?
options: Yes, it is a type of malware
No, they are two different things
cards.answer: Yes, it is a type of malware
cards.explanation: Malware is the general word. The virus, the ransomware and the Trojan horse are types of it.

cards.question: What is a Trojan horse (Trojan)?
cards.answer: A Trojan horse is malware hidden inside a program that looks useful. You install it yourself without knowing.
cards.explanation: Like in the legend: the gift hides the soldiers.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual tells how, in 2017, a CCleaner update contained a Trojan horse: more than 2 billion downloads were reported.

cards.question: What is ransomware?
cards.answer: Ransomware is malware that encrypts your files to lock them. The attacker asks for money to give you the key.
cards.explanation: A ransom is money demanded to set something free.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions ransomware as a threat to the availability of data.

cards.question: All your files are locked. A message asks for money to unlock them. Which malware is this?
options_why: A virus copies itself from file to file. Here, the goal is to lock files and ask for money.
A Trojan horse hides inside a program. Here, the demand for money points to ransomware.
cards.answer: Ransomware
cards.explanation: Locking files in return for money: that is the mark of ransomware.

cards.question: What is phishing?
cards.answer: Phishing is a trap message that copies a trusted source. It pushes you to click or to give a password.
cards.explanation: Phishing sounds like fishing: the message is the bait.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual says phishing is the most common form of social engineering, by email.

cards.question: What is spam?
cards.answer: Spam is an unwanted message sent to many people at once. Some spam messages are phishing traps.
cards.explanation: Spam is not always dangerous, but you should be careful with its links.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual talks about spam when it covers the CAN-SPAM law: unsolicited messages.

cards.question: A fake website asks for your password: phishing or ransomware?
cards.answer: Phishing
cards.explanation: The goal is to make you give away your secret. Ransomware, on the other hand, locks your files.

cards.question: What is social engineering?
cards.answer: It means tricking a person, by pretending to be someone else, to get information. Example: a fake call from the IT team.
cards.explanation: The attacker aims at the person, not the machine.
cards.explanation_more: According to the official manual, phishing is the most common form of it.

cards.question: What is a denial of service (DoS)?
cards.answer: A denial of service blocks access to a service by overloading it with requests. Real users can no longer use it.
cards.explanation: Nothing is stolen: the service is only stopped from answering.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions it as a common attack on availability.

cards.question: [[Ransomware]] encrypts your files and asks for money for the [[key]].
cards.answer: Ransomware encrypts your files and asks for money for the key.
cards.explanation: Encrypt, lock, demand: remember these three verbs.

cards.question: What is a distributed denial of service (DDoS)?
cards.answer: It is a denial of service launched from a very large number of computers at once. It is harder to stop.
cards.explanation: Blocking one single source is no longer enough: there are thousands.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions DDoS next to ransomware among the attacks that threaten the continuity of a business.

cards.question: What is credential theft?
cards.answer: It means stealing a username and password to pretend to be someone. Phishing is one way to do it.
cards.explanation: With your credentials, the attacker walks in through the front door.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions credential theft among the acts that aim at the secrecy of data.

cards.question: Which type of attack is it?
cards.answer: Phishing or social engineering: the fake message and the call. Malware: the virus and the ransomware. Denial of service: the two overloaded websites.
cards.explanation: Tricking a person, causing harm with a program, or overloading a service: three families.

items.text: A message copies your bank and asks for your password
A person pretends to be the IT team on the phone
A file copies itself into other files when you open it
A program locks your files in return for money
Millions of requests overload a ticket website
A website cannot be opened because of a flood of requests

cards.question: What is network sniffing?
cards.answer: It means secretly listening to the data that travels on a network. Encryption stops the listener from understanding it.
cards.explanation: The listener changes nothing: they only read what passes by.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions it among the malicious acts that aim at the secrecy of data.

cards.question: Why does phishing work even against careful people?
cards.answer: Because it plays on emotions: fear, urgency, curiosity. Under pressure, people click before thinking. The message also copies a trusted sender.
cards.explanation: Slowing down and checking the sender is the best habit.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual says phishing can get past even the most sophisticated security tools.

cards.question: Lea gets an email from the “director”: he asks for an urgent money transfer and says to tell no one. What should she do?
options: Check in another way, like a phone call
Make the transfer fast so the director does not get angry
Reply to the email to ask if he is sure
options_why: Urgency and secrecy are classic signs of manipulation.
Replying to the same email may send the question back to the attacker.
cards.answer: Check in another way, like a phone call
cards.explanation: A second trusted channel lets you check the request.

cards.question: What if just one employee clicks on a trap link?
cards.answer: Malware can install itself on their computer, then spread through the whole network. One single mistake is enough.
cards.explanation: One single click can open the door to the whole company.

paragraphes: You spent three hours on a homework assignment. The computer crashes, and everything disappears.
If you had kept a copy somewhere else, you would have lost five minutes, not three hours.
This spare copy is called a backup. It is one of the basic defenses in cybersecurity.

decouverte.comme: A castle has walls, guards at the gate, alarm bells and food supplies in case of a siege.
decouverte.enVrai: A company also stacks up defenses. The firewall is the guard at the gate: it filters what comes in and out of the network. Antivirus software looks for malware. Logs record what happens.

decouverte.question: A flaw in a program is known, and its maker publishes an update that fixes it. What happens if you do not install it?
options: The flaw stays open to attackers
decouverte.answer: The flaw stays open to attackers
decouverte.explanation: Once a flaw is known, attackers know it too. Not updating means leaving a door open. “Nothing” is tempting, because you see no difference.

decouverte.comme: A camera at the entrance does not stop any theft. But after a theft, you can watch again what happened.
decouverte.enVrai: Logs record who did what, and when, on a system. They do not stop an attack. They help you spot it and understand what happened.

decouverte.texte: A company finds that all its files are locked. It pays nothing: it has a backup from the day before, kept outside the network. In a few hours, it puts its files back. Without a backup, it would have lost years of work.

cards.question: What is a backup?
cards.answer: A backup is a copy of your data kept somewhere else, so you can get it back after a loss. Example: a copy of your files on another disk.
cards.explanation: It protects against breakdowns, theft and ransomware.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual recommends keeping several copies, including one away from the main site.

cards.question: What does it mean to restore?
cards.answer: To restore means to put data back in place from a backup. Example: getting your files back after a breakdown.
cards.explanation: A backup you do not know how to restore is useless: you need to practice.

cards.question: Does a backup help stop an attack or recover from it?
cards.answer: Recover from it
cards.explanation: It blocks nothing, but it lets you get your data back after the problem.

cards.question: What is a firewall?
cards.answer: A firewall is a filter that lets data pass or blocks it between two networks, following rules. Example: stopping strangers from entering a company's network.
cards.explanation: Like the guard at the gate of a castle: it checks who passes.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions the firewall among the technical controls, and requirement 1 of PCI DSS asks for a firewall to protect card data.

cards.question: What is antivirus software?
cards.answer: Antivirus software is a program that finds and removes malware. It must stay up to date to recognize new ones.
cards.explanation: An antivirus forgotten for months protects badly.
cards.explanation_more: Requirement 5 of PCI DSS, quoted in the manual, asks for antivirus software that is used and updated regularly.

cards.question: An attachment contains a virus. Which tool finds and removes it?
options_why: Logs record what happens, but they remove nothing.
The backup keeps a copy of the data, but it does not remove the virus.
cards.answer: The antivirus
cards.explanation: Finding and removing malware is the job of the antivirus.

cards.question: What is a patch?
cards.answer: A patch is an update that fixes a flaw in a program. Installing it is called patching the program.
cards.explanation: Many attacks use flaws for which a patch already exists.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions scanning and patching for vulnerabilities as examples of good practice.

cards.question: What are logs?
cards.answer: Logs are the written records of what happens in a system: who logged in, when, and what they did.
cards.explanation: They stop nothing, but they let you investigate.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual recommends turning on security logs and reviewing them to spot suspicious activity.

cards.question: A [[firewall]] filters the network; an [[antivirus]] looks for malware.
cards.answer: A firewall filters the network; an antivirus looks for malware.
cards.explanation: The guard at the gate filters; the nurse treats what has already come in.

cards.question: What is an intrusion detection system (IDS)?
cards.answer: It is a tool that spots suspicious behavior and warns you. Its cousin, the IPS (intrusion prevention system), can also block it.
cards.explanation: The IDS is like an alarm: it rings, but it does not close the door.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual lists IDS/IPS among the technical tools of a security program.

cards.question: What is a penetration test (pentest)?
cards.answer: It is a simulated and authorized attack that looks for weak points before real attackers do. The results are used to fix the problems.
cards.explanation: You attack yourself to find the flaws before others do.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions penetration tests to check that the rules of a firewall are strict enough.

cards.question: Does this defense help to prevent, to spot, or to recover?
cards.answer: Prevent: the firewall and the patch. Spot: the logs and intrusion detection. Recover: the copy put back and the restored system.
cards.explanation: Before, during, after: three moments, three types of defense.

items.text: A firewall that blocks a stranger
A patch installed in time
Logs that show a strange login
An intrusion detection tool that warns you
Files put back from a copy
A system restored after a breakdown

cards.question: What is a security incident?
cards.answer: A security incident is an event that puts data or systems in danger. Examples: ransomware, a stolen account.
cards.explanation: When an incident happens, you spot it, limit it, then recover.

cards.question: What is redundancy?
cards.answer: Redundancy means doubling an important element. If one breaks down, the other takes over. Example: two internet connections.
cards.explanation: It is like having a spare wheel in the car.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions doubled electricity, water and internet connections, and sometimes several internet providers.

cards.question: Why install patches quickly?
cards.answer: A known flaw can be used by any attacker. Each day of delay leaves the door open for longer.
cards.explanation: Attackers also read the patch announcements.

cards.question: A company reads its server log and sees a thousand failed login attempts at three in the morning. What does this log show?
options: A possible attack to look into
options_why: A thousand refused attempts in the middle of the night are not a sign of good health.
Nothing in the log says the firewall has disappeared.
cards.answer: A possible attack to look into
cards.explanation: Logs are used to spot this kind of sign so you can react fast.

cards.question: What if the only copy of your backup was on the same computer?
cards.answer: A breakdown, a theft or ransomware could destroy the original and the copy at the same time. It is better to keep a copy elsewhere.
cards.explanation: A copy in the same place as the original does not protect against a problem that hits that place.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual asks that at least one set of backups be kept away from the main site.

concepts.name: Vulnerability, threat, attack: three words not to mix up

paragraphes: You leave on vacation and leave a window open. Nobody has come in yet. Still, a burglar walks past the house and looks at the window.
Three things already exist: an open window, a possible burglar and valuables inside. The theft has not happened yet.
Experts have a word for each one. The open window is a weakness, or vulnerability. The burglar is a threat.

decouverte.titre: The house and its three elements
decouverte.comme: The open window is a weak point. The burglar is a possible danger. When they really come in, that is the burglary.
decouverte.enVrai: A vulnerability is a weak point of a system. A threat is what can take advantage of it. The attack is the moment when someone really does. The valuables are the assets.

decouverte.question: A program has a known flaw, but nobody has used it yet. What should we call it?
decouverte.explanation: The flaw is a weak point: it is a vulnerability. With nobody using it, there is no attack yet. “Attack” is tempting because the word sounds scary, but nothing has happened.

decouverte.comme: The sky is gray and you forgot your umbrella. Rain is possible, and you will get wet if it falls.
decouverte.enVrai: Risk is the chance that a threat takes advantage of a vulnerability and harms an asset. It depends on probability (the chance that it happens) and impact (how bad the damage is). Without a vulnerability or without a threat, the risk goes down.

decouverte.texte: An employee keeps their password on a paper stuck to the screen: that is a vulnerability. A curious visitor is a threat. If the visitor writes the password down and logs in, that is an attack. The company's data is the asset in danger.

cards.question: What is a vulnerability?
cards.answer: A vulnerability, or weakness, is a weak point in a system that an attacker can use. Example: a program that was never updated.
cards.explanation: The vulnerability is in the system: it exists even if nobody uses it.
cards.explanation_more: Simple definition. The official definition from the manual comes later, in the galaxy on threats and risk (D1.11).

cards.question: What is a threat?
cards.answer: A threat is an event or a person that can cause damage. Examples: a hacker, a fire, an angry employee.
cards.explanation: The threat is not in the system: it is what can hit it.

cards.question: An office door that is not closed properly: a vulnerability or a threat?
cards.answer: A vulnerability
cards.explanation: The badly closed door is a weak point. The threat would be the person who could take advantage of it.

cards.question: When a threat takes advantage of a vulnerability, what is that called?
cards.answer: An attack. It is the moment when someone really uses a vulnerability to cause harm.
cards.explanation: Vulnerability, threat, attack: the weak point, the danger, then the action.

cards.question: What is an asset?
cards.answer: An asset is anything of value to an organization: people, machines, data. Example: the customer list.
cards.explanation: An asset is what you are trying to protect.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual says an asset is “anything of value”, and mentions people, property and information.

cards.question: Vulnerability, threat or asset?
cards.answer: Vulnerability: the outdated program and the password that is too simple. Threat: the ransomware and the angry former employee. Asset: the customer database and the servers.
cards.explanation: The vulnerability is the hole. The threat is what can slip through it. The asset is what you want to protect.

items.text: A program that was never updated
A password that is far too simple
A ransomware that is going around
An angry former employee
The customer database
The company's servers

cards.question: What is a risk?
cards.answer: A risk is the chance that a threat takes advantage of a vulnerability and harms an asset. It depends on probability and impact.
cards.explanation: Without a threat, or without a vulnerability, the risk is lower.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual says that risk sits where threats, vulnerabilities and assets meet.

cards.question: What is an insider threat?
cards.answer: An insider threat comes from someone inside: an employee, a former employee or a partner. It can be deliberate or caused by a mistake.
cards.explanation: An insider threat does not need to force the door: it already has a key.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual says the insider threat is often seen as a major security concern.

cards.question: A flood can destroy a datacenter: is it a threat or a vulnerability?
cards.answer: A threat
cards.explanation: The flood is a dangerous event: a threat. The vulnerability would be having no protection against water.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions floods, excessive heat and power failures among the environmental threats.

cards.question: Can a threat be accidental?
cards.answer: Yes. A breakdown, a fire or an employee's mistake are threats, even with no intention to cause harm.
cards.explanation: So you protect against mistakes and accidents, not only against hackers.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual says a threat can come from a person who harms an asset on purpose or by accident.

cards.question: A [[vulnerability]] is a weak point; a [[threat]] is a danger that can take advantage of it.
cards.answer: A vulnerability is a weak point; a threat is a danger that can take advantage of it.
cards.explanation: The open window and the burglar: two different things.

cards.question: What is a data breach?
cards.answer: A data breach is an incident where data is read or stolen without permission. Example: a customer list that ends up online.
cards.explanation: It is the possible result of a successful attack.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual describes it as a cybercrime where information is viewed or stolen without authorization.

cards.question: On a website, the administrator password was left as “1234”. What does “1234” represent?
options_why: A threat is what can take advantage of a weak point, like a hacker. Here, “1234” is the weak point itself.
An asset is what you protect, like data. Here, “1234” is the hole in the protection.
cards.answer: A vulnerability
cards.explanation: It is an easy-to-guess weak point: a vulnerability.

cards.question: Why fix a vulnerability even if nobody has used it yet?
cards.answer: Because a threat can appear later, without warning. Once the vulnerability is known, someone can take advantage of it at any time.
cards.explanation: It is better to close the window before the burglar arrives.

cards.question: Put the steps in order, from the vulnerability to the damage.
cards.answer: A vulnerability exists. An attacker discovers it. They use it: that is the attack. Data is stolen or locked. The company suffers damage.
cards.explanation: You can cut the chain at each step: fix the vulnerability, spot the attack, limit the damage.

items: A vulnerability exists in a program
They use it: that is the attack

cards.question: What if you fix all the known vulnerabilities: does the risk disappear?
cards.answer: No. Threats like breakdowns or mistakes are still possible, and new vulnerabilities can appear. The risk goes down, but never disappears.
cards.explanation: The goal is not zero risk: it is to make the risk acceptable.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual calls the risk that remains after protection measures residual risk.

concepts.name: The organization and the law (organization, law, audit)

paragraphes: At school, there are rules: no phones in class, and a school planner you must carry. Other rules come from the law, like going to school being required.
A company also lives with rules from several sources: its own, those of its partners and those of the state.
In security, you must know them all. Otherwise, you risk a penalty or losing the trust of customers.

decouverte.comme: At home, you follow your parents' rules. At school, the school rules. In the street, the law. They add up.
decouverte.enVrai: A company has its own internal rules, standards that many agree to follow, contracts with its partners and laws that are required. If they clash, the law comes before the rest.

decouverte.question: A company does not follow a law about its customers' data. What does it risk?
options: Nothing, a law is only advice
decouverte.explanation: A law is required. Ignoring it can cost a fine, which is a sum of money to pay, or a lawsuit. Simple advice, on the other hand, forces nobody.

decouverte.titre: The audit, like a car inspection
decouverte.comme: A car goes through an inspection. An expert checks the brakes and the lights, then notes what is wrong.
decouverte.enVrai: An audit is a check done by a person who verifies whether the company follows its rules. The auditor reads documents, asks questions and runs tests. Then they write a report.

decouverte.titre: A shop and its customers' data
decouverte.texte: A shop keeps the name, address and email of its customers. This is personal data. The shop must keep it secret. In Europe, a law lets customers ask for it to be deleted. If the shop does not follow this law, it risks a fine.

cards.question: What is an organization?
cards.answer: An organization is a group of people who work together toward a shared goal. Examples: a shop, a bank, a hospital.
cards.explanation: In this course, the word organization also covers government offices and charities.

cards.question: What is an employee?
cards.answer: An employee is a person who works for an organization and is paid by it. They have access to some information.
cards.explanation: From the director to the newest employee, everyone has a role in security.

cards.question: Why does an employee not have access to all the files of the company?
cards.answer: Because each person only needs some of the information. The more access there is, the more risk of a leak or a mistake.
cards.explanation: Every extra access is an open door for no reason.

cards.question: What is a contractor or vendor?
cards.answer: A contractor is an outside person or company that provides a service or a product. Example: a technician hired to set up a network.
cards.explanation: They may have access to information: so you must frame their work with a contract.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions contractors, consultants and vendors among the third parties to manage.

cards.question: What is a customer?
cards.answer: A customer is a person or company that buys what the organization sells. Their personal data must be protected.
cards.explanation: Losing customer data also means losing their trust.

cards.question: Employee, contractor or customer?
cards.answer: Employee: the accountant and the salesperson. Contractor: the outside technician and the consultant. Customer: the buyer and the company that orders.
cards.explanation: Who is paid by the organization? Who provides it a service? Who buys something from it?

items.text: An accountant paid by the company
A salesperson of the shop
A technician from an outside firm who came to repair the network
A consultant hired for three months
A person who buys a product on the website
A company that orders supplies

cards.question: What is a contract?
cards.answer: A contract is a written agreement between two parties that says what each one must do. Example: the contract with a cloud provider.
cards.explanation: You can rely on it if the other party does not respect the agreement.

cards.question: What is a policy (an internal rule)?
cards.answer: A policy is an instruction that the organization imposes on its employees. Example: locking your screen when you step away.
cards.explanation: The official manual calls it a policy.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual defines policies, standards, procedures and guidelines in the galaxy D1.8.

cards.question: A company promises a customer in writing to keep their files accessible. What is this agreement called?
options_why: A standard is a set of recognized rules, not an agreement between two parties.
An audit is a check, not an agreement.
cards.answer: A contract
cards.explanation: A written agreement between two parties is a contract.

cards.question: What is a standard?
cards.answer: A standard is a set of recognized rules that many organizations choose to follow. Example: the ISO 27001 standard.
cards.explanation: The state does not force it, unless a contract or a law asks for it.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual mentions ISO/IEC 27001 as a very widespread standard in security.

cards.question: What is a law?
cards.answer: A law is a required rule written by the state. Not following it exposes you to a penalty.
cards.explanation: The law applies to everyone in the country concerned.

cards.question: The ISO 27001 standard, in general: a choice of the organization or a requirement of the law?
cards.answer: A choice of the organization
cards.explanation: A standard is followed by choice, or because a contract requires it. Only the law applies to everyone.

cards.question: What is a fine?
cards.answer: A fine is a sum of money to pay when you did not follow a law.
cards.explanation: It is one of the possible penalties, along with a lawsuit and a loss of trust.

cards.question: What is an audit?
cards.answer: An audit is a check done by a person who verifies whether the organization follows its rules. It ends with a report.
cards.explanation: The auditor reads documents, asks questions and runs tests.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual describes these three methods: examine, interview and test.

cards.question: A [[law]] is required; a [[standard]] is followed by choice or by contract.
cards.answer: A law is required; a standard is followed by choice or by contract.
cards.explanation: The requirement comes from the state on one side, from choice or a contract on the other.

cards.question: What is personal data?
cards.answer: Personal data is information that lets you recognize a person: name, address, birth date. The law requires you to protect it.
cards.explanation: The more precisely a piece of data identifies someone, the more secret it must stay.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual uses the term PII (personally identifiable information), seen in the galaxy D1.1.

cards.question: What is compliance?
cards.answer: Being compliant means following the laws, standards and contracts that apply to the organization. The opposite is called non-compliance.
cards.explanation: Being compliant does not guarantee you are secure: it is only a first step.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual says compliance is a solid base, but only the first step toward security.

cards.question: An online shop loses a list of customers with names and addresses. Which consequence is the most likely?
options: A fine and a loss of trust
options_why: Names and addresses are personal data: the law requires you to protect them.
An update can fix a flaw, but it does not fix the consequences of lost data.
cards.answer: A fine and a loss of trust
cards.explanation: Lost personal data can cost money and the trust of customers.
cards.explanation_more: The official manual says organizations that lose the secrecy of their data risk penalties and damage to their reputation.

cards.question: Why is an audit useful even if everything seems to be going well?
cards.answer: Because an outside person sees what you no longer notice. They spot gaps before they become real problems.
cards.explanation: You get used to your own flaws: a fresh look helps.

cards.question: What if an organization follows all the standards, but ignores a law?
cards.answer: It is still breaking the rules: the law applies, even if the standards are followed. Standards help, but they do not replace the law.
cards.explanation: You respect the law first, then you add the standards.
